passages: [prose] Recorded species were characterised following the functional classification of Kitahara and Fujii (1994, 1997). On the basis of resource utilisation patterns by species, these authors proposed a classification according to 2 fundamental niche dimensions (time and food). Applying the generalist/ specialist concept to the analysis of butterfly community structure, they classified butterfly species based on 2 representative traits: larval resource breadth (range of host-plant species used by larvae) and voltinism (number of generations per year). They considered host-plant specificity as an indicator of the niche breadth in a larval food dimension, while the notion of voltinism was extended to serve as a surrogate for the niche breadth in a seasonal time dimension (see Kitahara and Fujii 1994, 1997). This classification resulted in 4 functional groups: (i) typical specialists (TS) which are uni- or bivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 1 plant family only; (ii) typical generalists (TG) which are multivoltine species (3 generations or more per year) that feed on hostplants belonging to 2 or more plant families; (iii) rebound specialists (RS) which are multivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 1 plant family only; and selective generalists (SeG) which are uni- or bivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 2 or more plant families (see Online Resource 1) (Santin 2004; Lafranchis 2000; Tolman and Lewington 1999).

[prose] Over the 2 years of the butterfly survey, 2459 individuals of 41 species were recorded within the 15 urban parks studied (see Online Resource 1 for species list). Among these 41 species, 12 TG species (1745 individuals), 5 RS species (268 individuals), 7 SeG species (289 individuals) and 17 TS species (157 individuals) were recorded.
